summary: Concrete 1933 tower on an 1894 post light at Bush Point, Whidbey Island, in Admiralty Inlet: a Coast Guard light with the tower closed and the grounds disputed.

structures.type: square pyramidal, with gallery and no lantern
structures.note: 20 ft (6 m), per Rowlett and LighthouseFriends. The 1894 post light is not described as a tower.

staffing.note: Controlled from the residence of a caretaker, who is not named in the sources.

access.note: Tower closed (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett). Rowlett says the site is open. The Whidbey News-Times says the light stands on private property and may be photographed only from the road. The sources disagree on the grounds.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (owner and site manager per Rowlett and LighthouseFriends)

events.note: Tubular-lantern post light established by the Lighthouse Board; dated 10 May 1894.

The armored cruiser USS Colorado ran aground in fog on Puget Sound on 15 August 1908, on Liplip Point, roughly opposite Bush Point (LighthouseFriends). The Seattle Star said the cruiser was laid up for repairs.
$10,000 allotted for an automatic acetylene light at Bush Point (LighthouseFriends).
Reinforced concrete pyramidal tower finished; semiautomatic light and fog signal controlled from a caretaker's residence; project cost $6,197.
Fire damaged the tower and destroyed an adjacent structure, an inn (LighthouseFriends photo caption; Whidbey News-Times).
Compressed-air horn replaced by a diaphragm horn (Whidbey News-Times).
Fog signal discontinued; the tower still shows a light (LighthouseFriends; Whidbey News-Times).

keepers.name: John Farmer
keepers.note: Named by the Whidbey News-Times as the owner of the private kerosene lamp at Bush Point (a chicken and cattle farmer who lived from 1860 to 1910). LighthouseFriends says the private light was maintained by the Farmer family. Not a Lighthouse Service keeper. No years of service are given.

corrections.why: The 1894 date is the post light. The concrete tower was finished in 1933 (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett's directory; the USLHS record's tower year is 1933 too). Wikidata's first_lit of 1933 is consistent with this.

Rowlett lists the light as active, LighthouseFriends says the tower still exhibits a light, and the Whidbey News-Times says the Coast Guard still maintains it. The USLHS record's 'Active Aid to Navigation?: No' is the only contrary source. The Light List was not read; an editor should check it before applying.

corrections.current: 1989 built (Tower 3, from Rowlett's Gig Harbor (3) entry)
corrections.why: Rowlett's 1989 date belongs to the Gig Harbor (3) light, not to Bush Point. Rowlett's Bush Point entry has no Tower 3.
Gig Harbor is a different light, in the town of that name, and Rowlett lists it separately as Gig Harbor (3).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1894 date is the Lighthouse Board's tubular-lantern post light; the 1933 date is the concrete tower that replaced the private light and the post light. Both are sourced.

LighthouseFriends and Rowlett say the light is still exhibited or active; the USLHS record says it is not. The story reports the disagreement. The proposed correction in corrections above is for the editor to check against the Light List.
Rowlett gives a white flash every 2.5 s; LighthouseFriends says the light was on for five seconds and then off for five seconds. The record's 2.5 s stays until the Light List is checked.

LighthouseFriends' coordinates are used. Wikidata's point is about 2 km to the south-east. Rowlett places the light at the end of Lighthouse Way and Lake Avenue, which matches LighthouseFriends' directions.

notes_for_editor: No USLHS keeper roster exists for Bush Point (the place record lists none), and the corpus holds no keeper names. The only named person is John Farmer, from the Whidbey News-Times (2022); LighthouseFriends says only 'the Farmer family'. The caretaker of the 1933 light is not named anywhere read. The Whidbey News-Times says the light is on private property, while LighthouseFriends and Rowlett say the Coast Guard owns it; the story reports both and does not settle it. The Whidbey News-Times also says that all three of Mukilteo, Admiralty Head and Bush Point were lit by oil lamps lit by keepers; that does not fit Bush Point's private lamp and no-keeper history, so it was not used. The Commissioner's entry is a request for money in the detailed estimates, not evidence the work was done; the 1933 completion, the 1930 allotment and the $6,197 cost rest on LighthouseFriends, with the Whidbey News-Times agreeing on 1933 and the cost. The LighthouseFriends location for the 1908 grounding (Liplip Point) is not confirmed by the Seattle Star page read, which gives only 'during a fog on the Sound'. The Board's 1908-09 annual report, which LighthouseFriends cites for the $41,600 request, is not in the corpus and was not read. The 1894 entry's OCR reads 'post lighty Admiralty Inlety'; its printed page is not confirmed by the corpus (p. 7?), so the story cites scan p. 310 only. The Light List entry (the record's 2.5 s characteristic and 7.6 m focal height) was not read; Rowlett gives a 25 ft (7.5 m) focal plane and a 2.5 s flash. The 1945 fire and the inn's name are not used: the inn is described without naming it or its owners.
